title: How Minification Works to Reduce File Size
summary: Explains what minified code is, why CDN-hosted libraries like jQuery and Bootstrap look like unreadable walls of text, and how a minifier tool shrinks JS or CSS by stripping whitespace and comments.

concepts.heading: What minification is
points: Opening a CDN URL for jquery.min.js (or the Bootstrap CSS) shows a dense blob. That is the minified build: the same code with spaces, line breaks, indentation and comments removed.
It is still valid JavaScript (for jQuery) or CSS (for Bootstrap). Reformatting it with line breaks and indentation reveals the ordinary code.
Browsers ignore whitespace and comments, so shipping them only wastes bytes.

concepts.heading: Why minify
points: Smaller files download faster, which matters most on slow connections.

Demo: a minifier website (minifier.org) takes pasted JavaScript or CSS and outputs the compressed version. The sample drum-kit script went from about 1539 bytes to about 1113 bytes, saving roughly 426 bytes, even with just one added comment.
(Extra) Real minifiers also shorten local variable names, which saves more; savings grow with file size.

concepts.heading: Library distributions
points: Libraries ship two versions: a readable, uncompressed one for developers who want to study or customise the source, and a minified one meant for the browser.
If you do not need to edit the library, drop the minified file in (or link the CDN version).
If you customise the source, you can minify it yourself afterwards.
(Extra) Minified files usually carry .min in the name (jquery.min.js); keep your own source readable and minify only for production.

code_examples.caption: (Extra) Same logic, readable vs minified

pitfalls: Do not hand-edit a minified file; edit the readable source and minify again.
Comments you rely on will vanish after minification, so keep an unminified original.

gaps_and_ideas: Could fold into the jQuery loading lesson as an explore demo: a textarea where pasted JS is stripped of comments and whitespace, showing byte counts before and after.
